items.prompt: What is an application's "attack surface"?
choices: Every point where an attacker can send input to, or receive output from, the system
Only the login page and password reset flow
The total number of servers the application runs on
The size of the codebase in lines of code
items.explanation: Attack surface covers every endpoint, form field, header, and dependency that can receive input or expose output — far more than just the login flow.

items.prompt: A company adds a new internal admin API. Does this change its attack surface even if only employees are told the URL?
choices: Yes — any reachable endpoint is part of the attack surface, whether or not its URL is publicized
No — attack surface only includes endpoints listed in public documentation
No — attack surface only grows when a new server is provisioned
Yes, but only after the endpoint appears in a search engine
items.explanation: Attack surface is about what's reachable, not what's advertised — an unlisted endpoint is still part of the attack surface, which is exactly how the Scenario's stale staging route got exploited.

items.prompt: What is "injection" as an OWASP Top 10 category?
choices: Untrusted input is interpreted as code or commands by a downstream interpreter instead of being treated as inert data
An attacker physically accesses a server and installs malware
A dependency has a known, unpatched security vulnerability
A user is tricked into clicking a malicious link
items.explanation: Injection is specifically about the boundary between code and data breaking down — a database, shell, or template engine running attacker-supplied text as instructions rather than plain data.

items.prompt: Which of these is the clearest example of an injection vulnerability?
choices: A search box builds a SQL query by directly concatenating the user's search text into the query string
An endpoint returns any invoice by id without checking who owns it
A server ships with a debug endpoint still enabled in production
A password is stored using a fast, unsalted hash
items.explanation: String-concatenating user input directly into a query is the textbook injection pattern — the database can't distinguish the user's text from actual SQL syntax.

items.prompt: What does "broken access control" mean?
choices: A system correctly identifies who a user is, but fails to enforce what that specific user is allowed to do or see
A system fails to identify who a user is at all
A system's TLS certificate has expired
A system logs too much sensitive data
items.explanation: Broken access control is specifically an authorization failure, not an authentication failure — the system knows who's asking, it just doesn't correctly gate what they can reach.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, why could the attacker read any customer's invoices?
choices: The endpoint checked that a session was valid, but never checked whether that session's user owned the requested invoice
The attacker cracked the bcrypt password hashes
The TLS certificate was self-signed and untrusted
The JWT signing key had been leaked
items.explanation: The breach happened through a missing ownership check, not a cryptographic weakness — the endpoint authenticated the request but never authorized it against the specific resource.

items.prompt: What is "security misconfiguration"?
choices: A system is insecure because of how it's set up — a stale endpoint, a default credential, a permissive setting — rather than a logic bug in the code
A system is insecure because its encryption algorithm is mathematically broken
A system is insecure because a developer wrote a SQL query incorrectly
A system is insecure because a user chose a weak password
items.explanation: Misconfiguration is about setup and defaults, not application logic — the vulnerable code itself can be fine while the deployment or settings around it are the actual gap.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of security misconfiguration rather than injection or broken access control?
choices: An old staging build with a debug admin route was never removed before going to production
A search field's text is concatenated directly into a SQL query
An endpoint returns another user's data because it never checks resource ownership
A dependency has a publicly known, unpatched vulnerability
items.explanation: A leftover debug route being reachable in production is a setup/deployment problem, not a flaw in any single piece of application logic — the defining trait of misconfiguration.

items.prompt: The Scenario's company had strong hashing, TLS, and signed sessions, but still got breached. What does this show?
choices: Getting a few security fundamentals right isn't the same as being secure against all ten OWASP Top 10 categories
Strong hashing and TLS are actually unnecessary if a company has good session management
The breach proves bcrypt is a weak hashing algorithm
The breach proves TLS certificates should be rotated more often
items.explanation: The company closed off the cryptographic-failures and authentication-failures categories, but the breach came through a completely different category (broken access control) that those fixes never touched.

items.prompt: Why couldn't the attacker's exploit in the Scenario have been prevented by stronger password hashing?
choices: The exploit never involved passwords at all — it was a missing ownership check on an endpoint, unrelated to how credentials are stored
Stronger hashing would have prevented it, but the company used an outdated algorithm
The attacker did in fact crack the password hashes first
Password hashing and access control are actually the same OWASP category
items.explanation: The invoice endpoint was reachable by any authenticated session regardless of password strength — the gap was entirely in authorization logic, a different category from cryptographic failures.

items.prompt: If a system has strong crypto, strong auth, and TLS everywhere, does that mean it's secure against the OWASP Top 10?
choices: No — those cover only three of the ten categories; the other seven can still be exploited
Yes — crypto, auth, and TLS are the three hardest categories, so the rest follow automatically
Yes, as long as the TLS certificate is renewed on time
No — but only injection remains as a risk once those three are covered
items.explanation: Cryptographic failures, authentication failures, and (partially) transport security are three specific categories — access control, injection, misconfiguration, and the rest are independent risks that strong crypto and auth don't address.

items.prompt: This unit's L2 table marks some categories as "covered elsewhere in this track" and others as new to this unit. What does that distinction mean?
choices: Categories like cryptographic failures and authentication failures have their own dedicated units elsewhere in the security track; injection, broken access control (IDOR), and SSRF are this unit's own deep-dive focus
The "covered elsewhere" categories are less important than the ones in this unit
Every OWASP category needs its own dedicated unit, and this table lists which ones are missing entirely
The distinction is arbitrary and doesn't reflect the actual roadmap
items.explanation: The table is a map of where each category's depth actually lives across the track — this unit goes deep on three categories that don't already have dedicated coverage, while referencing where the others are handled.

items.prompt: Per L2's model of how an attacker actually picks a target, do they usually start by attacking the system's strongest defense?
choices: No — attackers look for whichever category has the cheapest exploitable gap, not the most impressive target
Yes — attackers are motivated to prove they can break the hardest thing first
No — attackers always start with social engineering regardless of the system
Yes, but only in penetration tests, never in real breaches
items.explanation: Real attackers are economically motivated — they map the attack surface and exploit whichever category is cheapest to break, which is almost never the system's strongest defense.

items.prompt: Why does it matter, for prioritizing security work, that attackers pick the cheapest gap rather than the hardest target?
choices: Investing everything into hardening one category while leaving another completely unchecked doesn't reduce risk proportionally — the breach comes through whichever category was left weakest
It means teams should only invest in the single most expensive-to-fix category
It means prioritization doesn't matter, since attackers are unpredictable
It means the cheapest category to fix should always be fixed first, regardless of its actual risk
items.explanation: If risk concentrates wherever the weakest category is, then over-investing in one already-strong area while neglecting another leaves the overall system just as exploitable as before.

items.prompt: Which three OWASP Top 10 categories does this unit's L3 go deep on with real vulnerable-then-fixed code?
choices: Injection, broken access control, and server-side request forgery (SSRF)
Cryptographic failures, authentication failures, and insecure design
Security logging failures, supply chain security, and secure-by-design
All ten categories, each with a full worked code example
items.explanation: L3 deliberately focuses on the three categories not already covered by dedicated units elsewhere in the track — injection, broken access control, and SSRF — rather than attempting all ten.

items.prompt: Does this unit claim to give full code-level depth on all ten OWASP Top 10 categories?
choices: No — three categories get real code in this unit's L3; the rest are mapped at a glance and pointed to their own dedicated units or later units
Yes — every category gets a full vulnerable-then-fixed code example in L3
No — this unit intentionally skips code examples entirely and stays conceptual
Yes, but only for the categories rated "critical" by OWASP
items.explanation: Depth tracks what's actually new here — three categories get full code treatment, while categories already covered (or covered later) elsewhere in the track are referenced, not re-explained.

items.prompt: Per L2's failure modes, what's the risk of treating "secure" as a single yes/no property?
choices: A system is secure against specific categories to varying degrees — a vague "we did a security review" says nothing about which categories were actually covered
There's no risk — "secure" is always a binary outcome in practice
It only matters for compliance certifications, not real breach risk
It's risky only if the review was done by an external vendor
items.explanation: Security is category-specific, not a single property — a review that covered crypto and auth says nothing about whether access control or misconfiguration were checked.

items.prompt: L2 warns against fixing "the category that's easiest to demo" instead of the one that's actually weakest. What's an example of this failure mode?
choices: Over-investing in a visible security banner or compliance certificate while an unglamorous category like access control stays untested
Spending equal time on all ten categories regardless of actual risk
Hiring a penetration testing firm to check every category
Patching a dependency with a known CVE as soon as it's discovered
items.explanation: Visible, demoable controls can create a false sense of coverage while genuinely risky but unglamorous categories — like access control or misconfiguration — go unchecked.

items.prompt: Fix buildSearchQueryFixed so it returns a parameterized query instead of concatenating the search term directly into the SQL string.

tests.description: sql uses a placeholder, not the raw term
tests.expr: expect(buildSearchQueryFixed("widget").sql).toBe("SELECT id, name, price FROM products WHERE name LIKE ?")

tests.description: params carries the wrapped search term
a SQL-injection-style term stays inert as data

items.explanation: The `?` placeholder and the term now travel to the database as separate things — fixed SQL syntax and an opaque data value — so the term can never change the shape of the query, no matter what characters it contains.
items.reference:
❌ Concatenation — user text becomes part of the SQL string itself
✅ Parameterization — user text travels as a separate data value, never as SQL syntax

Why: the database can't tell code from data unless the boundary between them is structural, not just visually careful.

items.prompt: Fix filterByCategoryFixed so it returns a parameterized query instead of concatenating the category directly into the SQL string.

tests.description: sql uses a placeholder, not the raw category
tests.expr: expect(filterByCategoryFixed("tools").sql).toBe("SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE category = ?")

tests.description: params carries the category value
a SQL-injection-style category stays inert as data

items.explanation: Same fix as any other injection point: the category value travels as data through the params array, never as text spliced into the SQL string, so it can't be interpreted as SQL syntax.
items.reference:
❌ Concatenation — user text becomes part of the SQL string itself
✅ Parameterization — user text travels as a separate data value, never as SQL syntax

Why: the database can't tell code from data unless the boundary between them is structural, not just visually careful.

items.prompt: Fix getInvoiceFixed so it also verifies the invoice belongs to the requesting user, not just that the session is valid.

tests.description: owner can read their own invoice
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { invoices: [{ id: 1, ownerId: "alice" }, { id: 2, ownerId: "bob" }] }; return getInvoiceFixed(db, { userId: "alice" }, 1).ownerId; })()).toBe("alice")

tests.description: non-owner is blocked from another user's invoice
tests.expr: expect(() => { const db = { invoices: [{ id: 1, ownerId: "alice" }, { id: 2, ownerId: "bob" }] }; getInvoiceFixed(db, { userId: "alice" }, 2); }).toThrow()

tests.description: unauthenticated requests are still rejected
tests.expr: expect(() => { const db = { invoices: [{ id: 1, ownerId: "alice" }] }; getInvoiceFixed(db, null, 1); }).toThrow()

items.explanation: One extra comparison turns "any valid session reads any invoice" into "a valid session reads only invoices it owns" — the missing authorization check, not authentication, was the actual gap.
items.reference:
🔑 Authentication — is this a real, logged-in user?
🚪 Authorization — is this specific user allowed to see this specific resource?

Why: checking only the first question and skipping the second is exactly what an IDOR is.

items.prompt: Fix getOrderFixed so it also verifies the order belongs to the requesting user, not just that the session is valid.

tests.description: owner can read their own order
tests.expr: expect((() => { const db = { orders: [{ id: 10, ownerId: "carol" }, { id: 11, ownerId: "dave" }] }; return getOrderFixed(db, { userId: "carol" }, 10).ownerId; })()).toBe("carol")

tests.description: non-owner is blocked from another user's order
tests.expr: expect(() => { const db = { orders: [{ id: 10, ownerId: "carol" }, { id: 11, ownerId: "dave" }] }; getOrderFixed(db, { userId: "carol" }, 11); }).toThrow()

tests.description: unauthenticated requests are still rejected
tests.expr: expect(() => { const db = { orders: [{ id: 10, ownerId: "carol" }] }; getOrderFixed(db, undefined, 10); }).toThrow()

items.explanation: Same shape as the invoice endpoint: authentication alone never implies authorization for a specific resource, so the ownership comparison has to be explicit.
items.reference:
🔑 Authentication — is this a real, logged-in user?
🚪 Authorization — is this specific user allowed to see this specific resource?

Why: checking only the first question and skipping the second is exactly what an IDOR is.

items.prompt: Implement isPrivateOrLinkLocalIP so it correctly flags loopback, private, and link-local address ranges (including the cloud metadata address).

tests.description: cloud metadata address is flagged
a public IP is not flagged
loopback is flagged
192.168.x private range is flagged

items.explanation: The cloud metadata service lives at a fixed link-local address (169.254.169.254) that's only meant to be reachable from inside the server's own network — blocking that range is what stops SSRF from leaking temporary cloud credentials.
items.reference:
🌐 Public IP — reachable from anywhere, safe to fetch
🔒 Private/link-local IP — only meant to be reachable from inside the server's own network

Why: a server-side fetch of a user-supplied URL can reach internal addresses the attacker's own browser never could.

items.prompt: Implement isPrivateOrLinkLocalIP so it correctly flags loopback, private, and link-local address ranges, including the boundary of the 172.16-31.x range.

tests.description: 10.x private range is flagged
172.20.x is inside the private range and flagged
172.32.x is outside the private range and not flagged
a public IP is not flagged

items.explanation: The 172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255 private range only spans the second octet from 16 to 31 — getting that boundary wrong either blocks legitimate public addresses starting with 172, or lets private ones through.
items.reference:
🌐 Public IP — reachable from anywhere, safe to fetch
🔒 Private/link-local IP — only meant to be reachable from inside the server's own network

Why: a server-side fetch of a user-supplied URL can reach internal addresses the attacker's own browser never could.

items.prompt: Fix fetchUrlPreviewFixed so it blocks non-http(s) protocols and blocks internal/private hostnames before fetching.

tests.description: cloud metadata URL is blocked
non-http(s) protocol is blocked
a normal public https URL is fetched

items.explanation: Two independent checks close two different classes of the same mistake: the protocol check stops non-HTTP schemes like file:// or gopher://, and the IP check stops HTTP requests aimed at internal-only addresses.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Restrict the protocol to http/https
2️⃣ Restrict the destination to non-internal addresses

Why: restricting only one of "what kind of request" and "where it can go" still leaves the other half of SSRF open.

items.prompt: Fix fetchUrlPreviewFixed so it blocks non-http(s) protocols and blocks internal/private hostnames before fetching.

tests.description: gopher protocol is blocked regardless of hostname
an internal 10.x address is blocked
a normal public http URL is fetched

items.explanation: Blocking gopher:// (or file://, etc.) closes off protocols that were never meant to be reachable this way at all, independent of whatever hostname follows the scheme.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Restrict the protocol to http/https
2️⃣ Restrict the destination to non-internal addresses

Why: restricting only one of "what kind of request" and "where it can go" still leaves the other half of SSRF open.
